No mention of grey nomads as state planning authority gives hybrid wind project the all-clear

Rachel Williamson
Nov 11, 2026
  • Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)Facebook
  • Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window)WhatsApp
  • Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window)LinkedIn
  • Share on Reddit (Opens in new window)Reddit
  • Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window)Bluesky
Battery Policy & Planning Wind
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:38
Instaread

There was no mention of grey nomads in the latest move to green-light the massive Baldon wind project in southern New South Wales (NSW), in decision so final that all merit appeals against the project are forbidden.

The 1,400 megawatt (MW) wind project with up to 200 MW and 800 megawatt-hours (MWh) of storage now has all planning approvals in hand and, crucially, this cannot be challenged in court. 

The project, in the South West renewable energy zone (REZ), was sent into the Independent Planning Commission (IPC) sin bin in September after receiving 73 objections during the normal planning process. 

But this time, it went through as a ministerial request for a public meeting, a process that means a decision has to be wrapped up in 10 weeks but all parties lose the right to a merit appeal in the courts afterwards. 

Luckily for proponents Goldwind Australia and Omni Wind Farm Pty Ltd, the IPC only imposed four extra conditions and beefed up another. 

The little-used power in NSW was first invoked for renewable energy projects in March, when planning minister Paul Scully asked for the Dinawan, Bullawah and “packet of poo tickets” Winterbourne wind projects to be hastened through. 

The decision came as absentee landlords and councils launched post-approval merit appeals against other wind projects to slow them down. 

The ill-fated Tamworth Regional Council suit against the Hills of Gold project was definitively roasted in court before being resolved with the council agreeing to provide the consent it believed it needed to give. 

But a suit by landowner Marshall Baillieu against the approval of the Valley of the Winds project is still waiting on the judge to publish their decision, and another against the Wallaroo solar farm, although dismissed in March, is also still winding its way through the courts. 

The project won grid connection approval in June, which was important as it was not one of the four to win access rights to the South West REZ and the 330 kilovolt Project Energy Connect transmission line. 

Flight of the grey nomads

Down in the South West REZ, the Baldon and other wind projects have the backing of councils and many residents. 

During the IPC hearings, Balranald Shire Council CEO Terry Dodds worried only about the prospect of traffic jams damaging the town’s reputation as a scenic stopover for grey nomads – retiree caravanners. 

“What we’re concerned about is if the over-width/over-height loads go through at the wrong time and the caravaning traffic finds out about it and starts complaining on Facebook and places like that, that the caravaners will circumvent Hay and Balranald and Euston altogether,” Dodds said.

He said the 6.5 metre wide wind turbine tower parts, nearly double the 3..5 metre width of the highway lanes leading into town, mean taking out some of the beautification elements of the town for some time.

“That’s going to leave the centre of Balranald looking pretty ordinary.

“So, if the same thing happens with this wind farm… that’s going to take two years and there could be five trucks to six trucks a day every day for two years. That is going to create a fair bit of disruption if it’s not staged.” 

Extra details

The IPC didn’t leave the planning decision wholly untouched, adding extra conditions to the environmental plans, accommodation, water and jobs. 

It is requiring the proponents to join a regional working group that will manage and research plains wanderer birds in the area, given the 769 hectares of native vegetation that needs to be cleared will have an impact on the grasslands avian. 

It also wants Goldwind and Omni Wind Farms to provide a shuttle bus between the project and accommodation to keep cars off the roads, create a plan for the 35 jobs that will come after the project is built, and go deeper into how it will manage water use across the whole project. 

It has also, unusually, beefed up one of the original consent conditions around decommissioning by requiring a decommissioning and rehabilitation plan.

Baldon will be one of the first major wind projects in Australia to combine grid-forming wind energy generation with DC-coupled battery storage.

It is also one of two wind-battery hybrids to become the first winners of the federal Labor’s Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS), getting a berth among the 19 winners of the 7th CIS auction, alongside six much more common DC-coupled solar-battery hybrids.
